title: About
text:
My projects



My research career began at the University of Plymouth, England. I undertook a research assistantship with Dr. Judy Edworthy, where I first became acquainted with research into the design of auditory alerts. I completed my Bachelors and Masters thesis with her; the former focused on sounds in the chemical refinery industries, the latter on design of digital bike bells. The results from the study of bike bells ultimately influenced the design of a recently released digital bike bell from the globally prolific Trek bikes company.



A video from Trek demonstrating their scientifically-informed bell!










I featured in a news piece by Global News Toronto on the MAPLE Lab’s alarms research


Given the fulfilment I had from research into auditory alerts, I was delighted to join the MAPLE Lab, under the supervision of Dr. Michael Schutz. My research contributed to the lab’s project of taking a musically-informed approach to improving alarm efficacy in hospitals. I focused on comparing perception between sounds of differing timbre, finding whether a piano-like ‘percussive’ timbre could be of benefit in sound design. In combination with other studies from our lab, we set up a strong case for percussive sounds being easier to detect and less aversive for hospital staff.



To see my work in greater depth, take a look at my publications!

title: About
text:
Future
During the course of my studies, I came to be fascinated by the quantitative methods used as part of the scientific method. I became especially intrigued by the use of Bayesian inference for deriving logically sensible conclusions from data (which I employed as part of my Ph.D. thesis). Consequently, I am now transitioning into data science, such that I can focus on handling data, and the art of deciding how to analyse and present it.

title: Curriculum Vitae
text:
Psychology Ph.D. Graduate, specialising in auditory perception, psychophysics, and human factors.
My research largely focused on understanding our perception of musical sound and how this applies to the design of safety-critical auditory alarms.
To this end, I have employed numerous cognitive experimental methods, and a wide range of quantitative methods to derive meaning from subsequent data.
I am now keen to transition into user experience based research and data science.
